title: Solution Overview
content:
Introduction This workshop builds a pipeline for electricity data ingestion, quality validation, and analysis using the EIA Open Data API.
The local implementation has been completed using PowerShell. The next phase will port the logic to Python and deploy it on AWS using AWS SAM.
Problem Statement Hourly electricity data includes actual demand, forecast demand, and net generation.
Manual processing requires repeated API calls, file exports, validation, and result aggregation. Missing or duplicate records can affect analytical results.
The pipeline provides a consistent workflow:
Read the configuration. Collect data. Validate data quality. Analyze validated data. Export datasets and reports. If a step fails, the pipeline stops and returns an error code.
Data Scope Attribute Value Source EIA Open Data API API route electricity/rto/region-data/data/ Initial respondent CISO — California Independent System Operator Frequency Hourly Time zone UTC Unit Megawatthours — MWh Business key period + respondent + type Selected metrics:
Code Meaning D Actual electricity demand DF Day-ahead electricity demand forecast NG Net electricity generation The data represents electricity activity in the CISO balancing authority area in the United States. DF is supplied by EIA, not generated by a model trained by this project.
Local Implementation Components Component Purpose collect_data.ps1 Call the API and save JSON/CSV data check_data.ps1 Validate quality and completeness analyze_data.ps1 Compare D with DF and calculate MAE and WAPE run_pipeline.ps1 Coordinate the steps and stop on failure JSON configuration Define the respondent, metrics, period, and output filename prefix The -ConfigPath parameter selects a configuration at execution time without changing source code.
Quality Checks Validate required fields. Validate finite numeric values. Check respondents, metrics, and units. Detect duplicate keys. Detect missing hour–respondent–metric combinations. Detect records outside the configured scope. Analysis Identify hours with high electricity demand. Match actual demand and forecasts by timestamp. Calculate errors and absolute errors. Summarize MAE and WAPE. Export a comparison CSV and a JSON report. Verified Results Period Records Compared hours Quality validation September 1–30, 2026 2,160 720 PASS September 1–7, 2026 504 168 PASS Tested failure scenarios include duplicate records, missing records, an empty API key, and a nonexistent configuration file.
Successful pipeline runs finish with exit code 0; tested failure scenarios return exit code 1.
Proposed AWS Design Component Proposed service Scheduled execution Amazon EventBridge Scheduler Collection and processing AWS Lambda Data storage Amazon S3 Table metadata AWS Glue Data Catalog Analytical queries Amazon Athena Logs and monitoring Amazon CloudWatch API key storage AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store — SecureString Permissions AWS IAM Infrastructure deployment AWS SAM / AWS CloudFormation S3 data is expected to be organized into the following areas:
raw/: Original data received from the API. clean/: Standardized data that passes validation. quarantine/: Rejected data requiring investigation. reports/: Quality reports and analytical outputs. The proposed Region is Singapore (ap-southeast-1). An architecture diagram will be added after the design is finalized.
Implementation Status The local processing pipeline has been completed, and its source code is managed on GitHub.
AWS deployment, API pagination, bounded retries, scheduling, Athena queries, and monitoring have not yet been implemented.
Source Code electricity-data-pipeline repository

title: Prepare the environment
content:
To prepare for this part of the workshop you will need to:
Deploying a CloudFormation stack Modifying a VPC route table. These components work together to simulate on-premises DNS forwarding and name resolution.
Deploy the CloudFormation stack The CloudFormation template will create additional services to support an on-premises simulation:
One Route 53 Private Hosted Zone that hosts Alias records for the PrivateLink S3 endpoint One Route 53 Inbound Resolver endpoint that enables “VPC Cloud” to resolve inbound DNS resolution requests to the Private Hosted Zone One Route 53 Outbound Resolver endpoint that enables “VPC On-prem” to forward DNS requests for S3 to “VPC Cloud” Click the following link to open the AWS CloudFormation console. The required template will be pre-loaded into the menu. Accept all default and click Create stack. It may take a few minutes for stack deployment to complete. You can continue with the next step without waiting for the deployemnt to finish.
Update on-premise private route table This workshop uses a strongSwan VPN running on an EC2 instance to simulate connectivty between an on-premises datacenter and the AWS cloud. Most of the required components are provisioned before your start. To finalize the VPN configuration, you will modify the “VPC On-prem” routing table to direct traffic destined for the cloud to the strongSwan VPN instance.
Open the Amazon EC2 console
Select the instance named infra-vpngw-test. From the Details tab, copy the Instance ID and paste this into your text editor
Navigate to the VPC menu by using the Search box at the top of the browser window.
Click on Route Tables, select the RT Private On-prem route table, select the Routes tab, and click Edit Routes.
Click Add route. Destination: your Cloud VPC cidr range Target: ID of your infra-vpngw-test instance (you saved in your editor at step 1) Click Save changes

title: Worklog
Project Proposal
content:
Building an Electricity Data Ingestion, Quality Validation, and Analytics Pipeline on AWS with Automated Deployment 1. Project Overview This project builds a pipeline to collect electricity data from the EIA Open Data API, validate its quality, store it, and provide datasets for analysis. The proposed system uses a serverless architecture on AWS, with infrastructure deployed through the AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM).
The initial scope focuses on the California Independent System Operator (CISO), covering three hourly metrics:
D — Demand: Actual electricity demand. DF — Day-ahead demand forecast: Electricity demand forecast for the following day. NG — Net generation: Net electricity generation. Timestamps are processed in UTC. Values retain the source unit provided by EIA: megawatthours (MWh).
2. Problem Statement Manually calling an API, downloading data, saving files, and validating records becomes difficult when data requires regular updates or processing across multiple periods. Missing hourly records, duplicate records, and invalid formats can affect analytical results.
The project proposes a consistent workflow to:
Collect data using configurable parameters. Validate data quality before analysis. Store original, clean, and rejected data separately. Track the status and errors of each execution. Support reruns and historical backfills. Recreate infrastructure using configuration code. 3. Project Objectives 3.1. Technical Objectives Build an EIA API collector supporting pagination, timeouts, and bounded retries. Separate respondent, metric, and time parameters from source code. Validate required fields, data types, duplicate keys, and hourly completeness. Store data in Amazon S3 using a structure suitable for queries. Use Amazon Athena to analyze the data. Configure scheduled execution, logging, and failure alerts. Deploy AWS resources using AWS SAM. 3.2. Analytical Objectives Identify hours with high electricity demand. Compare actual demand with the day-ahead forecast. Calculate forecast errors using MAE and WAPE. Observe changes in demand and net generation over time. DF forecasts are supplied by EIA, not generated by a model trained by this project.
4. Project Scope Component Scope Data source EIA Open Data API API route electricity/rto/region-data/data/ Initial respondent CISO Metrics D, DF, and NG Resolution Hourly Processing time zone UTC Test datasets September 2026 and September 1–7, 2026 Proposed historical coverage Up to 12 months, collected in smaller windows Proposed scheduled updates Daily, with a recent-window refresh to capture source revisions Deployment method AWS SAM The 12-month historical window is a proposed extension and may be adjusted after evaluating API behavior and actual costs.
The project uses aggregate U.S. electricity data. It does not represent Vietnamese electricity data or isolate electricity consumption by AI data centers.
Training a forecasting model and processing second-level streaming data are outside the initial scope.
5. Proposed Solution Architecture The system is expected to be deployed in the Singapore Region (ap-southeast-1).
Service / Tool Role Amazon EventBridge Scheduler Trigger scheduled collection tasks AWS Lambda Call the API, validate records, and standardize data Amazon S3 Store original data, clean data, rejected data, and reports AWS Glue Data Catalog Manage table metadata for queries Amazon Athena Query and analyze clean data Amazon CloudWatch Store logs, monitor execution metrics, and provide failure alarms AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store Store the EIA API key as a SecureString AWS IAM Manage access permissions for each component AWS SAM / AWS CloudFormation Define and deploy infrastructure as code Within the initial scope, AWS Glue is used for the Data Catalog. Glue ETL jobs are not currently planned.
Processing Flow EventBridge Scheduler triggers a Lambda task according to the schedule. Lambda reads the configuration and API key, then retrieves EIA API pages. Original data is stored in the S3 raw/ area without saving the API key or URLs containing it. Validation evaluates the structure, values, keys, and completeness. Valid data is standardized and stored in clean/. Rejected data is stored in quarantine/ with a report and is excluded from the clean dataset. Glue Data Catalog describes the data for Athena queries. Analytical outputs are stored in reports/ and used to generate charts. CloudWatch records execution status, record counts, and errors. Clean data is expected to be partitioned by respondent and UTC date, using Parquet to support queries.
Lambda is expected to access the public API without a VPC attachment. The initial architecture does not require EC2, a NAT Gateway, or a VPN.
An architecture diagram using official AWS icons will be added after the design is finalized.
6. Data Quality Validation The business key is defined as:
period + respondent + type
Validation rules include:
Required fields are present. Values can be converted to finite numbers. Respondents and metrics match the configuration. Units match the source dataset. Timestamps follow the required format and fall within the requested period. Business keys are unique. Every expected hour, respondent, and metric combination is present. No unexpected combinations occur. Missing values are not automatically replaced with zero. During scheduled execution, the system must account for source publication timing to distinguish unpublished data from collection failures.
Reprocessing Behavior Retain original data by collection run for comparison. Update clean data by business key or replace validated daily partitions. Avoid uncontrolled data appends. Support reloading failed periods or revised source data. 7. Analysis and Deliverables Analytical Questions Which hours have the highest electricity demand? How much does actual demand differ from the forecast? How does forecast error vary by date and hour? How do electricity demand and net generation change over time? Analytical Metrics MAE: The mean absolute error between actual demand and forecast demand. WAPE: The sum of absolute errors divided by the sum of absolute actual values, multiplied by 100%. A zero denominator is handled separately. These metrics describe differences in the supplied data. They do not establish causes or determine forecast quality under all conditions.
Proposed Deliverables Source repository and README. Sample configurations for different collection periods. AWS SAM template. Original data, clean data, and quality reports. Athena SQL queries. Charts showing demand and forecast errors. Test reports. Vietnamese and English workshop documentation. Deployment, operation, and resource cleanup instructions. Source repository:
electricity-data-pipeline
8. Current Progress Completed Built a PowerShell pipeline covering collection, quality validation, and analysis. Integrated the steps into a single execution command. Created JSON configurations and the -ConfigPath parameter. Successfully tested 2,160 records for September 2026. Successfully tested 504 records for September 1–7, 2026. Verified detection of duplicate and missing records. Verified that the pipeline stops when the configuration file does not exist. Exported quality reports and forecast comparison results. Managed source code using Git and published the repository and README to GitHub. Installed the AWS CLI and AWS SAM CLI. Not Yet Completed Confirm AWS CLI authentication and permissions. Port processing logic to Python for Lambda. Add pagination and retry handling. Complete the architecture diagram and cost estimate. Deploy project resources to AWS. Configure scheduling, Athena queries, and monitoring. 9. Implementation Plan Phase Main Activities Completion Criteria 1. Finalize the design Confirm scope, architecture, permissions, and cost Documented design and clear cost assumptions 2. Prepare AWS code Port logic to Python; add pagination, timeouts, and retries Correct handling of valid data and failure scenarios 3. Trial deployment Write the SAM template; create S3, Lambda, and the secret parameter One successful AWS collection run with validated data 4. Analysis and operation Configure Data Catalog, Athena, Scheduler, and CloudWatch Query outputs and verified scheduled execution 5. Complete documentation Test reprocessing; add charts, documentation, and cleanup procedures Execution evidence and reproducible instructions The remaining phases are provisionally estimated to take 3–4 weeks, subject to test results and actual availability.
10. Budget and Cost Control Cost Estimate The estimate was prepared using AWS Pricing Calculator for Asia Pacific (Singapore), based on the following trial workload:
AWS Lambda: 1,000 invocations/month, 512 MB memory, and an assumed average duration of 60 seconds/invocation. Amazon S3: 1 GB storage, 10,000 write/list requests, and 10,000 read requests/month. Amazon Athena: 100 queries/month, scanning approximately 0.1 GB/query. Amazon CloudWatch: 0.1 GB of logs/month and 1 standard alarm. AWS Glue Data Catalog: 1,000 objects and 10,000 access requests/month; no Glue ETL jobs or crawlers. Amazon EventBridge Scheduler: 30 invocations/month. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store: 1 Standard parameter and 1,000 API interactions/month. AWS KMS: 1,000 symmetric requests/month, using the default AWS managed key for Parameter Store. The Calculator displays approximately USD 0.32/month, equivalent to USD 3.84 over 12 months, with no upfront cost.
The estimate includes Free Tier allowances where applied by the Calculator, including Lambda. It is based on the assumptions above, excludes taxes, and does not represent a spending limit. Actual costs may change with data growth, pipeline reruns, or configuration changes. Existing lab resources are excluded from this estimate.
A separate USD 10–15 contingency budget is planned for the trial phase.

title: Test the Gateway Endpoint
content:
Create S3 bucket Navigate to S3 management console In the Bucket console, choose Create bucket In the Create bucket console Name the bucket: choose a name that hasn’t been given to any bucket globally (hint: lab number and your name) Leave other fields as they are (default) Scroll down and choose Create bucket Successfully create S3 bucket. Connect to EC2 with session manager For this workshop, you will use AWS Session Manager to access several EC2 instances. Session Manager is a fully managed AWS Systems Manager capability that allows you to manage your Amazon EC2 instances and on-premises virtual machines (VMs) through an interactive one-click browser-based shell. Session Manager provides secure and auditable instance management without the need to open inbound ports, maintain bastion hosts, or manage SSH keys.
First Cloud AI Journey Lab for indepth understanding of Session manager.
In the AWS Management Console, start typing Systems Manager in the quick search box and press Enter: From the Systems Manager menu, find Node Management in the left menu and click Session Manager: Click Start Session, and select the EC2 instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. This EC2 instance is already running in “VPC Cloud” and will be used to test connectivity to Amazon S3 through the Gateway endpoint you just created (s3-gwe).
Session Manager will open a new browser tab with a shell prompt: sh-4.2 $
You have successfully start a session - connect to the EC2 instance in VPC cloud. In the next step, we will create a S3 bucket and a file in it.
Create a file and upload to s3 bucket Change to the ssm-user’s home directory by typing cd ~ in the CLI Create a new file to use for testing with the command fallocate -l 1G testfile.xyz, which will create a file of 1GB size named “testfile.xyz”. Upload file to S3 bucket with command aws s3 cp testfile.xyz s3://your-bucket-name. Replace your-bucket-name with the name of S3 bucket that you created earlier. You have successfully uploaded the file to your S3 bucket. You can now terminate the session.
Check object in S3 bucket Navigate to S3 console. Click the name of your s3 bucket In the Bucket console, you will see the file you have uploaded to your S3 bucket Section summary Congratulation on completing access to S3 from VPC. In this section, you created a Gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to upload an object. The upload worked because the Gateway endpoint allowed communication to S3, without needing an Internet Gateway attached to “VPC Cloud”. This demonstrates the functionality of the Gateway endpoint as a secure path to S3 without traversing the Public Internet.

title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.
